Bridge the Gap: City Heights Youth Opportunity Initiative

The Problem

Two neighborhoods, one district, very different resources

City Heights and La Jolla are both part of San Diego Unified School District and receive the same base funding per student under California's Local Control Funding Formula. The difference in what students actually get access to comes from somewhere else: community fundraising power.

City Heights

  • 17 public schools serving mostly low-income, immigrant, and refugee families
  • No City Heights school in this study has a confirmed PTA/foundation revenue figure on public record
  • Hoover High offers 9 AP courses
  • Only 1 of 18 surveyed families took part in PTA/fundraising activity this year

La Jolla

  • 5 comparison schools in a wealthier, coastal neighborhood
  • Over $1.9 million in confirmed PTA/foundation revenue across just 3 schools
  • La Jolla High offers 19 AP courses and a decades-long competitive robotics/academic program
  • Active, professionally run PTA/foundation with dedicated staff and donor pages
What we're testing: if City Heights schools had the same fundraising support La Jolla schools have, students there would have access to the same AP classes, clubs, and programs — this isn't a public-funding problem, it's a community-fundraising-power problem.
The Evidence

What the data shows

Findings come from three sources: public financial records (IRS Form 990s, AP Course Ledger, School Accountability Report Cards), a district-wide ArcGIS map of all 162 SDUSD schools, and a bilingual survey of 18 City Heights families.

La Jolla schools report $1.9M in confirmed PTA/foundation revenue. No City Heights school has a confirmed figure on public record — which reflects missing data, not a measured zero.
Hoover High (City Heights) offers 9 AP courses; La Jolla High offers 19.
Survey respondents' household income skewed toward the middle of the range — no one reported under $25,000.
Only 1 of 18 surveyed families took part in PTA/fundraising activity — and that family was in the highest income bracket.
44% of families didn't know whether their child's school offers at least one AP/Honors or robotics/sports/arts program.
Interactive Tool

District-wide ArcGIS dashboard

To check whether the City Heights/La Jolla gap is a two-neighborhood coincidence or a district-wide pattern, the same PTA/foundation research was expanded to all 162 SDUSD schools.

Open Live Dashboard →

What it shows

  • Only 29 of 162 SDUSD schools (18%) have a confirmed PTA/foundation revenue figure on public record
  • Confirmed revenue is clustered almost entirely in wealthier, coastal neighborhoods — led by La Jolla High ($937K) and La Jolla Elementary ($680K)
  • City Heights fits the wider district pattern rather than standing out from it
  • Districtwide, confirmed PTA/foundation revenue totals about $5.6 million — mostly at high schools ($2.9M) and elementary schools ($2.3M)

Who it's for

  • Parents & PTA volunteers — compare your school to nearby ones
  • PTA/foundation leaders — use it as evidence when applying for grants
  • District administrators — target equity-focused support
  • Researchers & advocates — a citable public snapshot of fundraising equity

The Project

About this study

This is a capstone project for BDA 603: Smart Cities and Sustainability at San Diego State University, researched and produced by Swasthika Rajendran under the guidance of Dr. Gabriela Fernandez.

It combines a virtual ethnography of City Heights, public financial and academic records, a district-wide GIS analysis, and a bilingual family survey to test one specific hypothesis: that the opportunity gap between City Heights and La Jolla schools comes from community fundraising capacity, not from unequal public funding.

It ties directly to UN Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) and Goal 10 (Reduced Inequalities).
